chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Yazid Sha'ir, from Harun ibn Hamzah, from 'Abd al-A'la, who said:

I said to Abu 'Abdillah (عليه السلام): 'The one who leaps upon this matter, claiming it for himself—what is the proof against him?' He said: 'He is to be questioned about the halal (permissible) and the haram (forbidden).'

He said: Then he turned toward me and said: 'Three proofs do not come together in anyone except that he is the صاحب of this matter: that he be the most entitled of the people in relation to the one before him, that the weapon be with him, and that he be the possessor of the manifest testament—such that, when you arrive in al-Madinah, you ask the common people and the children about it: To whom did so-and-so leave his bequest? They will say: To so-and-so son of so-and-so.'

key_terms.السِّلَاحُ: the weapon, a sign of transmitted authority
key_terms.الْحَرَامِ: what is forbidden in the Sacred Law
key_terms.الْحَلَالِ: what is permissible in the Sacred Law
key_terms.الْمُتَوَثِّبُ: one who seizes or leaps upon authority without right
key_terms.الْوَصِيَّةِ الظَّاهِرَةِ: the clear and publicly known testament of succession
key_terms.هَذَا الْأَمْرِ: this matter, referring here to the Imamate

ai.seo_question: How does this hadith describe the proofs for recognizing the true Imam and refuting false claimants?
ai.summary: This hadith sets out criteria by which a false claimant to the Imamate is exposed and the true Imam is recognized. It identifies knowledge of halal and haram, precedence and nearness to the previous Imam, possession of the weapon, and the publicly known testament as signs of the rightful divine authority.
